rv.q: But we also feel the warmth of his friendship with fellow ex-con Jim (a twinkly Everal Walsh), as well as his conflicted sense of responsibility for his brain-damaged brother, Gabriel, played by Simon-Anthony Rhoden with wild-eyed innocence, who believes that his trumpet-playing will open the gates of Heaven for the worthy.
Conviction and powerful authority are the hallmarks of every performance in this fizzing and compelling masterwork.
In Daniel Bailey’s hands, it’s visceral, intense and arresting.
The production is one of the stronger examples of regional theatre collaboration having first opened at Leeds Playhouse with a short future stint also planned at HOME Manchester.
A longitudinal story that provides much insight into post-war America: well worth seeing.
This striking new production makes many of its issues relevant today, giving audiences plenty to reflect on long after the curtain falls.
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ A powerful, moving family drama with outstanding performances, exploring love, betrayal and the scars of the past.

Director Daniel Bailey has made us really feel emotionally involved with this family and we can celebrate Troy Maxson as one of American playwriting great tragic heroes along with Willy Lomax, Eddie Carbone and Joe Keller.
Wilson's Fences is a respectful, well-acted take on a landmark play.
For a production with music hardwired into its core, it lacks the pacing and range to make for an engaging and worthwhile three hours.
Headlong’s revival of Fences is impressively honed, with the simmering first act infusing significance into the explosive second.

cn.t: Wilson's powerful family drama receives largely strong reviews for its visceral intensity and outstanding performances, though one critic finds the production lacking in energy despite its promising start.
